opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a lot, probably more than people admit when they're excited about a hot market. A startup is a long, painful process, and the main thing you have early on is an unfair advantage. For most technical founders, that advantage is the thing you've already spent years getting really good at.

For me, it was computer graphics and high-performance computing. I spent years in that area, writing simulators and compilers and thinking about how to make physics run fast on GPUs. So when I thought about starting a company, it made sense to build around that. I understood the problem deeply, I knew the users because I had been one of them, and I had credibility in that community. That combination is hard for someone coming in from outside to copy.

But I'd add two caveats. First, being good at something isn't enough. You have to check whether there's real demand for it. A lot of technical people, including me, fall in love with the technology and assume the market will follow. Sometimes it doesn't, or it takes much longer than you expect. So you should treat your expertise as a starting point and then go talk to users very honestly.

Second, your skills should match the hardest part of the company, not just the most interesting part. If the real bottleneck is sales or distribution and you're purely a technical person, you either need to learn that quickly or find a co-founder who's great at it.

So I'd give it heavy weight, maybe the single biggest factor, but always combined with real market validation and a willingness to grow beyond what you're already comfortable doing.

r001.rationale: The response says prior expertise is a major advantage, but does not say that being relatively good in the domain is sufficient or that exceptional ability is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It says outsiders may find the founder’s combination of expertise, user familiarity, and credibility hard to copy, but does not state that founders with entirely unrelated education, networks, and experience have a very low chance of success.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it deserves a lot of weight, but probably not in the way most people expect. For me, the starting point was never "what is the market opportunity" in the abstract. It was: what have I spent years actually suffering through, where I know the problem better than almost anyone else?

Taichi came out of my PhD work in graphics and physical simulation. I wrote a lot of GPU code, I knew exactly how painful it was to get high performance out of these systems, and I knew how many researchers were stuck using Python for convenience while wanting C++ or CUDA speed. That was not a thesis I came up with from reading industry reports. It was a wound I had personally. So when the time came to think about a company, the direction was almost obvious, because I had a decade of accumulated context that gave me an unfair advantage.

That said, I would separate two things. There is what you are technically good at, and there is what the market needs. Being good at something gives you the right to attempt the problem, but it does not guarantee that the problem is worth solving for anyone else. A lot of technical founders, myself included at times, fall in love with the elegance of the solution and underestimate how much work it takes to turn that into something people will adopt and pay for. So I would say use your expertise to pick the domain, because that is where your intuition is sharp and your learning curve is already behind you. But then be very honest and very humble about the parts you are not good at, whether that is sales, product, or understanding the user who is not like you.

The other thing I'd add is that "what you are good at" is not fixed. When I started, I was good at compilers and simulation. I was not good at hiring, fundraising, or talking to customers. A founder has to be willing to become good at new things quite fast, and the existing strength is really just the seed that buys you the time and credibility to grow the rest. If you only ever stay inside your comfort zone, the startup tends to stay a research project.

r001.rationale: The response says relevant expertise gives a founder an advantage and a right to attempt a problem, but it does not state that being relatively good is sufficient without exceptional ability.

r002.rationale: The response describes the advantage of Hu’s own relevant experience, but does not state that founders have a very low chance of success when their education, network, and experience are entirely unrelated.

astra-6.text:
I think it deserves a lot of weight, but it shouldn’t be the only thing you consider. What you’re already good at gives you a starting advantage. You can move faster, and you may recognize opportunities that other people miss. But being good at something doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a business there. You still need to understand who needs it and why they would pay for it.

I’d look for the overlap between what you’re good at, what you’re curious enough to keep working on for years, and what people actually need. And I wouldn’t treat your current skills as a fixed boundary. As a founder, you’re going to have to learn things you’re not good at. Your strengths should help you get started, rather than determine everything you’re allowed to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response calls existing strengths a starting advantage, but does not say that being relatively good in the relevant domain is sufficient or that exceptional ability is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss education, networks, or experience being unrelated to a startup, or state that this would make success unlikely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you should give it a lot of weight, but it shouldn’t be the only consideration. Being good at something gives you a head start—you can move faster, and you may see opportunities that other people miss. But that doesn’t automatically mean there’s a business there. You still need to understand who has the problem and whether they care enough to pay for a solution.

So I would look for the overlap between what you’re good at, what you’re excited to keep working on, and what people actually need. And I wouldn’t treat your current skills as fixed. You can learn new things. The question is whether your existing strengths give you a useful advantage as you learn.
